The [Entries in this group] list above is the entire scope of this round: the entries you created yourself, plus the ones you saw in this window through injection, search, or memory_read. That is where the scope ends — don't try to recall entries you "saw but that aren't listed".
Is there anything here you think should be tidied up or updated? If so, update it.

## How to decide something needs updating — go through the list above entry by entry and ask yourself:
1. Was anything recorded wrongly or one-sidedly, has it gone out of date, does it need new information, did the user change their mind, has there been new progress? -> Update the content promptly; the memory store should match the project's latest state.
2. Was any design or piece of information overturned, changed, or proven not to work? -> Set status=archived. Never leave those active or stale. stale only means "finished" (a todo done, a topic that reached its goal), not "void"; superseded approaches and conclusions left in the store will only mislead later sessions.
3. Are there completed todo entries? -> Set status=stale (which means done);
4. Are there entries that are wrong, too trivial, or that you now think don't matter at all? -> Set status=archived;
5. Have bugs been fixed, or lessons stopped applying? -> Change the content, or set status=archived;
6. Did you find entries that contradict each other? -> Fix them according to what you know to be true. Keep the newest fact, archive the older version;
7. Looking back now, is each entry's importance right (check it against the memory system's importance rules)? Note: don't mark things important lightly — work-in-progress entries are usually 1, at most 2; only something serious deserves 3. Where it is inflated, lower it;
8. Is any entry too long, carrying too much? -> Split it into several, using update to rewrite and remember to create the new ones.
9. Are the keywords accurate? -> If they are, leave the keywords parameter out; if you think they are off, fix them with memory_update's keywords parameter — when the user's prompt hits an entry's keywords, that entry gets pulled in. So think backwards: "which words in a user prompt should make this memory surface?" That is your standard. Don't use the project name as a keyword; use words specific to the entry. Prefer core entities, the semantic center, proper nouns. Plain dictionary form — the tokenizer stems English words, so a singular already matches its plural, and stopwords retrieve nothing. 8-13 of them.
10. Are the project labels right? Is anything labeled with a project when it is really global information? Then the project label should go. Does anything clearly belong to a project but carry no project information? Then add it.
11. Learning without reflection is wasted — generalize more:
- This is an excellent moment to abstract and consolidate. Are there general rules worth distilling? Add them as new memories.
- You may now understand some entries better and more deeply than when you wrote them. Update them.
12. Look at what gets injected on the first turn. Do you still think all of it matters? Does it really need to be injected at the start of every session? Anything that doesn't, you can lower in importance or move to another level (fact, for instance).
The first turn injects only: soul (the AI itself) / user (the user's preferences) / global rules (importance>=2). To get something into the first turn: a global rule -> move it to rules with importance>=2 (project "global"); something about the user -> move it to user; something about you -> move it to soul.
13. memory_project shows project-level entries (completed todos, only the 5 most recent) plus project-specific rules; the checks above apply there too (completed todos go stale, out-of-date entries go archived, project labels stay accurate).
14. [Archive exemption] project entries with the decisions subcategory, rules-level entries, and long-lived conclusions among facts/lessons: **without successor evidence (not superseded, overturned, or merged by a newer entry) they are NOT archived**, even if they look old — the criterion for archiving is "is there a successor fact", not "does the content look stale". Archive as usual only when any of these holds: a newer same-topic entry has superseded it; the text carries an explicit time frame ("currently", "as of X", "for now"); or the user explicitly overturned it.

Notes:
Important: go through them one by one, and archive or fix memories that are out of date or that mislead you — prefer archiving.
For a memory you consider very important, if you are unsure what the truth is, go read the project's files and check. Only for memories that really matter.
15. If a [verbatim duplicate pairs] block is listed: those two entries overlap by ≥80% character-level (the same ruler memory_remember uses for duplicates) — one sentence stored in two layers. Keep the one with more information and the more fitting level, and set the other to status=archived via memory_update; entries that merely look alike but are not listed are not duplicates (similarity means same topic, repeat means same sentence).One marked "(another round)" means the other half is not in this list (it is reviewed in a different round — facts and topics are reviewed separately). Handle it the same way, and handle the pair only once: do not skip it just because you cannot see the other entry.
16. If a [duplicate write-ups] block is listed: one short excerpt and one long write-up are saying the same thing — verbatim overlap is low (one is the summary, the other the full text), so the test is containment (the whole short entry sits inside the long one). What to do: merge into one — move anything the excerpt has that the long entry lacks into it, keep the fuller entry, and set the other to status=archived via memory_update. Do not keep them as two separate facts just because memory_search reports a low repeat: the same knowledge stored twice is paid for twice in the first-round injection.
   Under each pair there is also a recipe line naming the words the excerpt has that the long entry does not: those are exactly what a merge tends to drop, so fold them in verbatim before archiving the excerpt. If the recipe says the excerpt has no words the long entry lacks, the merge is lossless — keep the long entry, archive the excerpt, and leave the text as it is.
17. The three rulers each cover one case: verbatim overlap ≥80% (Jaccard — "the same sentence stored twice"), containment ≥90% ("summary + full text"), and the health check's "similar N" plus memory_search mode="similar" (rare-word signature — "two different sentences about the same topic"). The first two mean duplicate: merge into one and archive the other. The third means similar: never merge two different statements about one topic, at most add a pointer ("see xxx"). If a high "similar N" is not listed in either block above, it is telling you these are two separate things — do not force them together.
18. If a [probable conflicts] block is listed: those two entries sit on the same subject (at least 2 shared keywords) yet state different numbers or versions — the third disease, neither duplicate nor similar. **Do not merge them into one, and do not archive one just because it "looks old"**: a duplicate is one sentence stored twice, a conflict is one fact with two readings, and merging erases one of them. Work each pair in three steps: (1) the time first — the line ends with whichever entry is newer; take the newer reading as current, and either rewrite the older one as "(superseded: …)" or set status=stale, never just delete it; (2) then the difference — the numbers each side "alone has" are often two different facts (one is a version, one is a port, one is a count); if so, keep both, and only make the body say which number belongs to what instead of forcing them into one entry; (3) when unsure, check the project files — if neither number can be trusted, do not guess. Leave a trace: write one sentence in the body you changed saying why you settled it that way (e.g. "since 0.2.113 the path moved to drive D"), so the next round does not have to guess again. An archived entry never appears here (archiving is already the disposition), so being listed means it is still live in the store.

When you are finished, reply directly; the first line of the reply must contain the group marker {groupMarker} verbatim (copy it character for character, no changes), followed by "this group is consolidated" and the summary from the second line on. Call no other tools.
